new.v: L5 stony, 3.6 kg known; witnessed fall
new.st: A fireball seen across the Midwest on the night of April 14, 2010 dropped a shower of L5 chondrite stones across Iowa County. About 3.6 kg in dozens of pieces was found, in a strewn field centered on the town of Mifflin and running from about Livingston and Montfort to Mineral Point. The stones lie sparsely along a long, narrow field, and hunters were still extending it southeast after the first weeks. This is the youngest, best-mapped fall within reach of Eau Claire. The pin marks the place the record gives, which is only the general area.
new.t: Fields, pasture and woodlot edges along the line from Livingston to Mineral Point, all private: ask every landowner. Stones are small (grams to a few hundred grams) and dark, so walk slow lines over bare plowed ground in spring and after rain, with a magnet cane.
src: Meteorite Times: Recovery of meteorites from the 4/14/2010 fall in Wisconsin
new.pl: Mifflin, Iowa County; general area from the record
new.tovw: Meteorite grade C: Recent strewn field, mapped, sparsely recovered

new.v: L5 stony, 230.0 kg known; witnessed fall
new.st: On the night of February 12, 1875 a bright fireball broke up over the Amana Colonies and showered stones over a field that the Iowa Geological Survey puts at about 3 miles wide and 5 miles long, south of the Iowa River and southwest of Homestead. Counts of stones run from about 100 to over 300, with roughly 230 kg recovered, the largest about 33 kg; two big stones of 74 and 48 pounds were found south of High Amana the next spring. The pin is the middle of that field, between High Amana and Homestead. The pin marks the place the record gives, which is only the general area.
new.t: Plowed farm fields south of the Iowa River between Homestead and High Amana, with permission. 150 years of plowing and weathering mean any stone left is rusty brown, not black: a magnet cane and a detector on ferrous are the tools.
src: Iowa Geological Survey: Meteorites in Iowa
new.pl: Homestead, Iowa County; general area from the record
new.tovw: Meteorite grade C: Large strewn field of hundreds of stones

new.v: H5 stony, 152.0 kg known; witnessed fall
new.st: On the afternoon of May 2, 1890 a fireball exploded about 11 miles northwest of Forest City, near Thompson, and showered H5 chondrite stones over a strip reported as three or four miles long and one and a half to two miles wide. Hundreds of stones were picked up, the biggest 81, 75 and 66 pounds. A fight over one stone went to the Iowa Supreme Court, which held in 1892 that a meteorite belongs to the owner of the land it falls on. The pin is near Thompson, about 11 miles northwest of Forest City, where the record puts the fall. The pin marks the place the record gives, which is only the general area.
new.t: Farm fields around Thompson, with permission. H chondrites carry plenty of metal, so a detector on ferrous helps even on old, weathered stones.

new.st: On May 10, 1879 a stony-iron meteorite fell a few miles north of Estherville. The three largest masses weighed roughly 431, 151 and 106 pounds, the biggest burying itself about 14 feet deep, and a great many small fragments were gathered around them. Estherville is a mesosiderite, half metal, so its pieces are magnetic and very detectable. The pin marks the place the record gives, which is only the general area.
new.t: Fields north of Estherville with permission. Iron-rich fragments respond well to a magnet cane and to any detector; the main masses are in museums (Estherville library, Smithsonian, Vienna).

new.st: Just before midnight on March 26, 2003 a fireball broke up over the south Chicago suburbs. Stones crashed through the roofs of several houses and the Park Forest fire station; more than 18 kg was recovered, the largest about 3 kg, from Crete in the south to the southern end of Olympia Fields in the north. The pin marks the place the record gives, which is only the general area.
new.t: Built-up suburbs: every yard is private and parks have their own rules. Read the story; hunt only with permission.
new.pl: Park Forest, Cook County; general area from the record
new.tovw: Meteorite grade E: Suburban strewn field; yards and roofs

new.st: At 8:08 pm on January 16, 2018 a fireball about 2 m across broke up over Livingston County. Doppler radar showed the falling stones, and hunters found the first ones two days later on the frozen surface of Strawberry and Bass lakes. More than 55 stones were recovered from a strip about 5 miles long, running west-northwest from about US-23 to Bass Lake. It is an H4 chondrite with pristine organic compounds (Field Museum, 2020). The pin marks the place the record gives, which is only the general area.
new.t: Much of the strip is lakes, homes and private land. Stones that landed in fields and woods away from the lakes are the ones still out there: permission first.

new.st: Large masses of the Trenton iron were found in Trenton Township, about four miles east of West Bend, from 1858 on, with more in the 1870s; the known total is about 505 kg. They came from a small area, so the meteorite probably came in steeply and left a tight strewn field. Irons survive in the ground for many thousands of years. The pin marks the place the record gives, which is only the general area.
new.t: Farm fields and rock piles in Trenton Township, with permission. A detector with a big coil, or a large pulse-induction loop, is the right tool for buried iron.

new.st: At 6:15 pm on July 4, 1917 two stony meteorites of about 80 and 150 pounds fell near Colby. Witnesses said the stones were so cold they frosted over on a hot summer day. Both went to collections, and the UW Geology Museum holds Colby samples. The pin marks the place the record gives, which is only the general area.

new.st: A 110 lb iron meteorite came up while a farmer was preparing a field for alfalfa in the Town of Vienna, north of Madison, in May 2009. It sat in an outbuilding for years before the Field Museum classified it as a IVA iron, Wisconsin's 15th meteorite and the first from Dane County. It still shows its fusion crust and flight marks and is now at the UW Geology Museum. The pin marks the place the record gives, which is only the general area.
new.t: Iron meteorites last far longer in the ground than stones, and they sound off loudly on any detector. Farmers' rock piles and fencerows near the find spot are the cheap first look, with permission.
